messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: question about stan modeling language
parts:
Hi, Bob. I have some questions following up on our mtg last week. The questions are, what happens under certain stan statements. I'm assuming there are four types of variables: data, parameter, derived quantity, index. I think I got some things wrong here so I'm setting it down so you can correct me.
A

1. x ~ norm (mu, sigma)
If x is data, this adds a term to the log posterior
If x is a parameter, this adds a term to the log posterior
If x is a derived quantity, this returns an error?
If x is

2. x <- y + z
If x is data, this does what?
If x is a parameter, this returns an error?
If x is a derived quantity, this tells stan to find all instances of "x" in the log posterior and replace it with "y + z". Also this tells stan to compute x as y+z and save it.
If x is an index, this returns an error?

3. x <- norm (mu, sigma)
If x is data, this returns an error?
If x is a parameter, this returns an error?
If x is a derived quantity, this tells stan to draw from a normal, use it to compute x and save it.
If x is an index, this returns an error?

As you can see, one of the difficulties here is that derived quantities are being used in two ways, sometimes as intermediate steps in a calculation or in a specification of a distribution, sometimes as things to be saved in their own right.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] question about stan modeling language
parts:
This is going to be a novel. Are we meeting Wednesday?
We can discuss more. I'm about to start writing the manual
as soon as I get the R interface done and it'll explain
all this from first principles.

1. There are four flavors of declarations:

constants: data & derived data
variables: parameters & derived parameters

and two ways in which variables arise outside
of declarations:

loop indexes (int)
lp__ log probability value (double)

Data and derived data is "constant" in that it
acts like "data" in the R2Bugs sense and variables
are variable in that they act like "parameters"
in the R2Bugs sense.

Everything pretty much follows from the way each
statement type is translated.

y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
-------------------------------------------
lp__ += normal_log(y,mu,sigma);

y <- x + log(z);
-------------------------------------------
y = x + log(z);

for (n in A:B) statement
------------------------------
for (int n = A; n <= B; ++n) {
statement'
}

where statement' is the translation of the statement
making up the body of the for loop.

The initial value of lp__ is the sum of the log absolute
Jacobian determinants of all the variables declared with
transforms. So if I declare

parameters{
double(0,) tau;
}
-----------
lp__ += tau; // log transform

and tau gets transformed from the value provided by HMC or
NUTS using exp(tau_unbounded).

Further, integers are separated from doubles,
vectors, row vectors and matrices are included and
any of these can be put into arrays and declared
with various constraints like boundedness or
positive definiteness.

There isn't nearly as much error checking as
you may be expecting because the user can correct
things that may look like errors in other ways (e.g.,
by applying the Jacobian to a transform). I'm mainly
checking well-formedness, existence of functions
and basic type compatibility.

For your case 1,

y ~ norm(mu,sigma);

what happens depends on which eight patterns of
constant/variable we have. Here's the actual code:

...
normal_log(const T_y& y, const T_loc& mu, const T_scale& sigma,
...
if (!propto
|| !stan::is_constant<T_y>::value
|| !stan::is_constant<T_loc>::value
|| !stan::is_constant<T_scale>::value)
lp -= square(y - mu) / (2.0 * square(sigma)); // SUMMAND 1
if (!propto
|| !stan::is_constant<T_scale>::value)
lp -= log(sigma); // SUMMAND 2
if (!propto)
lp += NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI; // SUMMAND 3

If we're not calculating proportionally, but fully, all three
summands get included. If we're calculating proportionally,
we drop

summand 3 always, because it's a constant normalizing term.

summand 2 if sigma is constant

summand 1 if all of y, mu and sigma are constant

Now keep in mind that any of y, mu or sigma can be a complex
expression involving other terms. Any arithmetic operation
involving variables returns a variable; arithmetic ops with
all constant arguments return a constant. So you can
literally write

log(tau[n]) ~ normal(alpha * x[n] + beta, sigma);

if you want and exactly the same as the above will happen.

Now if you go and write such a thing and tau[n] is a parameter
(i.e., an auto-dif variable) rather than data (i.e., a double),
then you have to increment the log probability with the
log absolute derivative of the transform.

Here, the transform
is p(tau[n]) = p(log(tau[n])) | 1/tau[n] |

you'll have to also add the log of the absolute
value of the derivative, which in this case is:

lp__ = lp__ - log(tau[n]);

Now you're good to go with parameter tau[n]. If we disallow
the first thing, we really cut down on the expressive power.
As is, you can just write out the whole density yourself by
increment lp__. Doing that, you have plenty of rope to hang
yourself.

2. x <- y + z just literally performs the assignment in
the order in which it is visited. It's illegal only if
x is constant and y or z is variable. Loop indexes are
treated just like any other variable, so if you write

for (n in 1:N) {
z[n] <- foo(x[n]);
n <- n + 1;
}

you'll only hit the odd numbers for n, assigning
z[1], z[3], z[5], ...

Variables and constants may be reassigned. So you can
do this:

for (n in 1:N) {
mu <- alpha * x[n] + beta;
y ~ normal(mu,1);
}

Each trip through the loop, mu has a different value.
This is OK even if one or more of alpha, x[n] or beta
are variables. This is a huge space savings on what
BUGS and JAGS require:

mu[n] <- alpha * x[n] + beta;
y ~ normal(mu[n],1);

You can still write it the BUGS way if you want.

If the left-hand-side is a parameter, it just gets
reassigned. You lose the original connection to the
log probability as a parameter and it acts just like
a new derived value. So you could save even more
space by finishing the calcuation with a parameter
that impacts the log probability, then reusing its storage.
(This won't save space, but I can see people trying it
and it'll do what they expect in acting like other local
parameter variables.)

3. Right now, x <- norm(mu,sigma) is illegal because
norm isn't declared as a function. I was thinking we could
add the random variate generators, at which point someone
could write:

x <- rnorm(mu,sigma);

and it'd generate a random draw from norm(mu,sigma) and
assign it to x as described in 2. The problem here is
that we don't want to auto-differentiate the random normal
generator, so I don't know how useful this will be as it'd
require either (a) mu and sigma to be constant data, or (b) it
to be "cut" in the BUGS sense so that the generation has no
bearing on the log probability function (this is what we
were talking about last time -- I'd thought before we could
do something more clever).

If Daniel's still reading at this point, we need overloaded
versions of rnorm that demote variables to constants, sort of
like we did the reverse for the matrix library for auto-dif.

Whew.

- Bob
